newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: FOCUS - OPEC freezes output to buoy oil prices.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - OPEC freezes output to buoy oil prices.

text.p: OPEC oil ministers agreed at Vienna talks on Wednesday to freeze current output quotas until the end of the year in an attempt to boost world petroleum prices.
Crude oil jumped on the news with the benchmark North Sea Brent Blend for August delivery ending up 34 cents in London at $18.21 per barrel. It briefly hit $18.45.
But longer-term, analysts said the market would demand firm proof that nations like Venezuela that have been violating quotas would honour promises given in Vienna to stop the cheating.
"And now the markets will judge," agreed Libya's cartel president Abdullah Salem al-Badri.

The accord that is being extended sets a ceiling on total volume by the Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries at 25.03 million barrels daily, including volume from Iraq under its food-for-oil deal with the United Nations.
But chronic violations have, in fact, lifted actual output some two million above the ceiling. And prices have sunk from $25 since January.
Announcing Wednesday's decision, OPEC secretary-general Rilwanu Lukman said that all 11 cartel members gave individual pledges that they would now adhere to mandatory limits.
Lukman said no threats had been made against alleged violators but that they had made promises to colleagues and OPEC believed them.

Some seasoned OPEC-watchers who were present in the lobbies were sceptical, among them U.S. oilman Oscar Wyatt who doubted whether fuel demand would be strong enough to lift prices if OPEC produces as much as it is likely to do.
"There is nothing to lift this market...it would have to be some external event other than consumption," said Wyatt, retiring chairman of Coastal Corp.
"People will not believe that anything has changed until they see it," said Leo Drollas, economist at the London-based Centre for Global Energy Studies.
Drollas said that Venezuela which is above quota by a huge 800,000 barrels daily "simply cannot deliver on a commitment like that".
Nigeria is another cash-pinched Third World country that monitors say is over-producing.
A strong line on violations by OPEC linchpin Saudi Arabia teamed with Gulf rival Iran took traders by surprise.

Venezuela's minister, Erwin Arrieta, was earlier on Wednesday summoned to a private session with Saudi Arabia's Ali Naimi and Gholamrezah Aghazadeh of Iran - which a Gulf delegate said was intended to "emphasise the need for quota compliance".
That sounded like OPEC parlance for a tongue lashing. But beyond that, OPEC has no mechanism to compel a sovereign state to honour its quotas.
Delegates said that Saudi Arabia was in no mood to threaten to turn up the taps on its huge spare capacity as a retaliatory measure.
The new OPEC accord is due to be rubber-stamped at a plenary session of the OPEC conference on Thursday.
